concepts.misconception: I think {x,p}={p,x}, since the Poisson bracket is symmetric like a dot product, so order of arguments does not matter
concepts.correctTyped: No — {x,p}=+1 while {p,x}=−1; the Poisson bracket is antisymmetric, {f,g}=−{g,f}, so swapping arguments flips the sign
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — {x,p}={p,x}, since the Poisson bracket is symmetric like a dot product, so order of arguments does not matter
concepts.typedSource: seed probe "Compute {x,p} and {p,x} for canonical position and momentum. Are they equal?" (isCorrect choice / misconception-tagged choice, verbatim)
concepts.offTopic: Is the transformation Q=q², P=p/(2q) canonical?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I can transform to any variables I want.
concepts.correctTyped: No — computing the Poisson bracket gives {Q,P}=1/2−1=−1/2≠1, so it fails the canonical test, despite being a smooth, well-defined coordinate change
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — any smooth, invertible coordinate transformation qualifies as canonical, since you can transform to whatever variables you want

concepts.offTopic: Is Hamilton's principal function S simply the numerical value of the action integral ∫L dt, computed for an already-known trajectory?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think i'll integrate L dt to get S.
concepts.correctTyped: No — S(q,α,t) is a function determined by solving the Hamilton-Jacobi PDE ∂S/∂t+H(q,∂S/∂q,t)=0, valid independent of whether the trajectory is already known; the trajectory is extracted from S afterward
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — S is just the action integral, computed by integrating L dt along a known path
